summary: This document lists security-related requirements for the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) protocol, which lets outside applications read and change a router's state. It supplements the I2RS architecture described in RFC 7921.

plainLanguage.summary: If outsiders can talk to a router, they need rules about who is allowed and how to keep the talk private. This lists those rules.

subtitle: Security requirements for the Interface to the Routing System protocol.

tldr.problem: The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) protocol allows external applications to read and modify the routing state in routers. This direct access poses security risks including unauthorized changes, identity spoofing, and data exposure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines security requirements across multiple dimensions: peer authentication, identity validation, transport security (both encrypted and constrained non-secure), role-based access control, and key management.
tldr.outcome: I2RS protocol implementations must follow these requirements to ensure that external applications can safely manage router state. The document supplements RFC 7921 (the I2RS architecture) and is a consensus standard of the IETF.

facts.label: Secure transports
facts.value: TLS, SSH, DTLS over secure protocols

today: RFC 8241 is an Informational RFC that remains the authoritative security requirements specification for I2RS implementations. It is referenced by router vendors and IETF working groups developing I2RS-compatible management protocols and data models.

sections.title: Secure Access to Routers
sections.content:
The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) is a new protocol that allows external applications (I2RS clients) to read and write information stored in a router (I2RS agent), changing the router's configuration and behavior in real time. This direct access to routing state is powerful but dangerous—a compromised client or an attacker posing as one could bring down the network, redirect traffic, or steal sensitive information.

RFC 7921 describes the I2RS architecture. This document focuses on its security requirements: how to identify and authenticate clients and agents, how to protect communications in transit, how to control what each client is allowed to do, and how to detect and respond to attacks. I2RS reuses security building blocks from existing IETF protocols (such as TLS, SSH, and DTLS) rather than inventing new mechanisms, but it adds some new features specific to router management.
sections.plainLanguage: A router controls where Internet packets go. I2RS lets programs ask a router to change the rules. Those programs must prove who they are, and the router must trust them.

sections.title: Components and Security Concepts
sections.content:
I2RS combines several existing IETF protocols. A secure transport (such as TLS or SSH running over TCP) encrypts and authenticates the connection. A management protocol (such as NETCONF or RESTCONF) runs on top of the secure transport and carries the router configuration and state information. Optionally, an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) protocol (such as Radius or Diameter, also over secure transport) distributes identity and role information to the agents and clients.

I2RS introduces two new concepts beyond these standard building blocks. A priority mechanism determines which client wins if multiple clients try to change the same piece of state simultaneously—the client with the highest priority succeeds, and the others receive an error. An opaque secondary identifier lets a single client identify which application is making a request (for example, a weekly configuration task versus an emergency change), improving traceability without requiring separate client identities.

I2RS also permits an optional non-secure read-only transport for public data (such as BGP route announcements or public telemetry), subject to strict controls. Write operations and configuration of notification streams must always use the secure transport.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS seals the conversation. NETCONF sends the commands. A priority system decides who wins when two programs disagree. An identifier tracks which program made each change.

sections.title: Peer Identity and Authentication
sections.content:
Every I2RS client and agent must have an identity and at least one unique identifier. Before any I2RS communication occurs, the client and agent must mutually authenticate—each must prove to the other that it knows the correct identity. This identity authentication happens at the secure transport layer (TLS or SSH), not just at the I2RS protocol layer.

Identity distribution (the process of loading identifiers into clients and agents) should happen outside the I2RS protocol, typically before the protocol connection is established. AAA protocols may be used for this, but other mechanisms are acceptable. Critically, if an AAA protocol distributes identity information, it must itself run over a secure transport (such as Radius over TLS or Diameter over TLS).

Once a secure transport session is established and identities are authenticated, the I2RS agent should assume the client's identity remains valid for the duration of that session. Similarly, the client should assume the agent's identity remains valid. Each message processed must be validated against the identity of the party that sent it, accounting for the fact that identity validation can be expensive and should be amortized across multiple messages on the same secure connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says 'I'm Alice' and proves it. The router says 'I'm Router-1' and proves it. They trust each other for the whole conversation.

sections.title: Secure and Constrained Transports
sections.content:
The secure transport is mandatory for all I2RS clients and agents. It must provide data confidentiality (encryption), data integrity (authentication codes), and practical replay prevention (so an attacker cannot record and replay old messages). The secure transport must be associated with a key management system that ensures only authorized parties can obtain encryption and decryption keys. Key management should normally be automatic (e.g., TLS handshake) rather than manual (hand-coded keys), except in constrained environments.

Write operations and configuration of event notification must always use the secure transport. Read operations may optionally use a non-secure transport, but only for data marked as nonconfidential—such as publicly available information like BGP route views or website status. The non-secure transport must not carry any data that identifies a person, and the I2RS data model must explicitly mark which data is suitable for non-secure transport.

I2RS requires Denial-of-Service (DoS) protection at both the transport and protocol layer. The secure transport achieves this through authentication and rate limiting. For non-secure transport, the I2RS higher-layer protocol must detect and warn of potential DoS attacks over a secure side channel.

I2RS can support multiple simultaneous secure transport sessions between the same client and agent, as long as the security implications are properly managed.
sections.plainLanguage: The secure channel scrambles messages so only the router and the program can read them. A separate public channel lets the program read obvious data like public traffic statistics, but nothing secret.

sections.title: Role-Based Access Control and Data Protection
sections.content:
I2RS uses role-based access control to manage permissions. Each authenticated client is assigned one or more roles, and each role has a scope: read-only, write-only, or notification (event subscription). A client with a read role can query the routing state; a client with a write role can modify configuration; a client with a notification role can subscribe to event streams.

When sensitive data (such as router configuration or traffic statistics) flows over a secure transport, the management protocol (NETCONF or RESTCONF) applies access control lists to enforce these roles. The transport layer protects the data in transit, and the higher-layer protocol protects it at rest in the router.

Role security must be enforced consistently even when a client uses multiple simultaneous transport connections to the same agent. The I2RS architecture defines how to track roles across multiple streams and connections so that an attacker cannot bypass access control by splitting requests across channels.

I2RS also defines a mechanism for message traceability (specified in RFC 7922) that logs which client and which secondary identifier made each change, supporting both audit trails and forensics of suspicious activity.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice has read permission for status and write permission for configurations. The router checks this for every request. The router also logs who did what, for auditing.

sections.title: Summary of Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC codifies security requirements across seven categories:

Peer identity authentication (SEC-REQ-01 to SEC-REQ-03): Clients and agents must have unique identifiers and mutually authenticate over the secure transport. Identity distribution happens outside the I2RS protocol.

Identity validation (SEC-REQ-04 to SEC-REQ-06): Every message received must be validated to confirm the sender's identity is valid and permitted for the requested action. Non-secure transports must validate that the content is appropriate for non-secure delivery.

Priority and redundancy (SEC-REQ-07 to SEC-REQ-08): Each client identity must have exactly one priority level. A client may have different secondary identifiers for different applications using the same client, allowing traceability of which application made each change.

Transport and confidentiality (SEC-REQ-09 to SEC-REQ-16): Secure transport is mandatory for write and event-configuration operations. It must provide encryption, integrity, and replay protection. Non-secure transport is optional for read-only nonconfidential data. Key management must prevent unauthorized parties from obtaining keys.

Management protocol security (SEC-REQ-17 to SEC-REQ-19): The management protocol must enforce access control and provide data integrity even on non-secure channels. Message traceability must be supported across both secure and non-secure communications.

Role-based security (SEC-REQ-20 to SEC-REQ-22): Role-based access control must be enforced consistently across multiple transport connections. If an I2RS client is tightly associated with a person, additional privacy protections are required.

Environment security (SEC-REQ-23): The I2RS protocol must be implemented in a secure environment, considering the security of the host system on which clients and agents run.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists 23 specific rules covering: who can prove their identity, what each person is allowed to do, how to keep secrets, and how to keep a log of changes.
